top.line: Cheap model reviews tip security towards open source
top.para: Open source had visible code but few reviewers; proprietary software had budget and cover. Models now run deep security reviews repeatedly at little cost, supplying the paid attention open source lacked. curl's year shows the shape, and security, sovereignty and maintenance as a business meet at the least amount of code in production.

in-short.line: Cheap eyeballs raise the bar and shrink production code
in-short.para: There was no clear winner until models made deep, repeated review cheap. curl went from noise to hundreds of real fixes, a quiet frontier scan and then deeper findings. The scale is real across labs and coalitions. Expect higher bars and fewer, better projects, with all incentives pointing at the least code in production.

balance.line: Open source lacked paid reviewers; proprietary code had cover
balance.para: Raymond's "enough eyeballs" argument always met the reality that eyeballs were missing: 60 percent of maintainers in Tidelift's 2024 survey were unpaid hobbyists, and slow deep reviews never happened. Proprietary software had budget plus the cover of hidden code. Open source's advantage was efficiency: public fixes sweep a bug's variants.

cheap.line: Model reviews made paid attention abundant for open source
cheap.para: Reviews that took a specialist weeks now take an afternoon and can rerun on every change, while hidden code is worth less. Anthropic's Glasswing scanned over 1,000 projects and estimated 6,202 high or critical vulnerabilities; Chainguard's Athena coalition reported 2,000 patches across 500 projects; DARPA's challenge systems found 18 real vulnerabilities.

curl.line: curl is getting harder to break, wave by wave
curl.para: curl ended its bug bounty on 31 January 2026 after reports became noise, then AI-assisted reports triggered two to three hundred fixes. A frontier scan in May found a single low-severity bug, yet deeper tools then produced thirty-five published vulnerabilities and curl 8.23.0 shipped 24 security fixes. Maintainers' time is now the bottleneck.

changes.line: Expect higher bars and fewer, better open source projects
changes.para: Findings will need more proof and contributions a higher standard, since anyone with a model can make small fixes. The long tail of tiny packages will shrink as small APIs are written in place. Human researchers, domain experts and maintainers remain, provenance matters more, and mission-critical code should be industrialised.

forces.line: Secure, sovereign and paid-for all point the same way
forces.para: Open source becomes secure through cheap review, required for sovereignty because you can only move what you can read and run, and paid for through maintenance: customers get a private repository with only the features they use and pay for it to be maintained. Open source is a licence, not a free-for-all.

least-code.line: Everyone now wants the least code in production
least-code.para: Customers want only the features they use, maintainers want the least to maintain, and security wants the least to review and attack. Removing what one use case never ran took a real tool from 1,500 files to 428. For the first time writers, sellers and securers of open source share incentives.

limits.line: No clean-project list; curl still has bugs; predictions remain
limits.para: No list of projects where AI found nothing could be found, so curl's story stands in. curl is not clean, only harder to break. Counts are the reporters' own, the cost and depth of model review are personal experience, and fewer, better projects and maintenance as business are predictions.

sources.line: Sources: Stenberg's curl posts and vendor security reports
sources.para: The piece comes from a voice memo of 14 October 2026, with quotes checked on primary pages. Sources include Daniel Stenberg's blog and curl's contribution rules, Anthropic's Project Glasswing update, Chainguard, Help Net Security on Athena, DARPA's AIxCC results, The Register on Tidelift and Raymond's The Cathedral and the Bazaar.
